target_audience: High School Students and Math Educators

sections.title: The Hook: The 'Confused Architect' Scenario
sections.content: Introduce the importance of a good explanation through a relatable character. If an architect gives vague instructions, the building falls. In math, if an explanation is poor, the logic collapses.
sections.example: Pip the Penguin is trying to build a slide. His friend says, 'Make it steepness-ish.' Pip is confused. This illustrates that 'intuition' without 'precision' fails.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: The Language of Math
sections.content: Before explaining, we must agree on 'Primitive Terms' and 'Logical Connectives'. An effective explanation assumes a baseline but defines the specific 'tools' being used for the current problem.
sections.example: Visualizing a 'Toolbox': Before explaining the area of a circle, we show the 'tools' we need: the radius (r), the constant (π), and the concept of 'squaring' (growing a 1D line into a 2D surface).

sections.title: Criterion 1: Visual-Symbolic Mapping
sections.content: A great explanation never leaves an equation floating in a vacuum. It maps every symbol to a geometric or physical representation. This is the 'Show, Don't Just Tell' rule.
sections.example: When explaining (a+b)², instead of just FOIL, show a large square divided into four sections: a square of a², a square of b², and two rectangles of ab. The visual 'proves' the algebra instantly.

sections.title: Criterion 2: Logical Cohesion (The Chain of 'Why')
sections.content: Each step must follow the previous one with a clear 'Because'. Effective explanations avoid 'It is obvious that...' and instead use logical bridges.
sections.example: An animation of a chain: Step A (Given) -> Link (Because of Property X) -> Step B (Result). If one link is missing, the explanation 'breaks'.

sections.title: Criterion 3: The Principle of Parsimony (Simplicity)
sections.content: The 'Ockham’s Razor' of math. An effective explanation uses the minimum number of steps required to reach the conclusion without sacrificing rigor. Avoid 'Math-ese' jargon where plain language suffices.
sections.example: Comparing two explanations of 'Slope'. Version A: 'The differential change in the ordinate relative to the abscissa.' Version B: 'How much you go up for every step you go right.' Version B is the more effective entry point.

sections.title: Application: Explaining the Pythagorean Theorem
sections.content: Combine all criteria into one 60-second master explanation. Use a character (Pip) to navigate the logic using visuals and minimal jargon.
sections.example: Pip places 3 square crackers around a right-angled triangle. He notices the area of the two smaller crackers perfectly fills the space of the largest one. Visual: Water pouring from two small square tanks into one large square tank.

sections.title: The Checklist: Summary & Review
sections.content: A final recap of the three criteria: 1. Visual Mapping, 2. Logical Cohesion, 3. Simple Precision. A call to action for the audience to test their own explanations.
sections.example: A 'Quality Control' stamp appearing over Pip’s final clear diagram, showing a green checkmark for each of the three criteria.
